title: Geometry-First Generative Spatial Single-Cell Reconstruction

problem.claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing provides large-scale cellular profiles but loses spatial context, while spatial transcriptomics preserves only partial spatial structure at lower resolution.

gap.claim: Existing integration methods commonly depend on spot deconvolution or mapping cells to a fixed measured spot lattice, limiting reconstruction flexibility, particularly in unpaired settings.

contributions.claim: GEARS reconstructs intrinsic single-cell spatial geometry guided by spatial transcriptomics without requiring cell-type labels, histological images, or cell-to-spot assignments.
GEARS combines a domain-invariant expression encoder with a permutation-equivariant diffusion-based generator and EDM-style refiner trained under pose-invariant supervision.

GEARS aggregates pairwise-distance predictions from overlapping cell subsets and solves a global distance-geometry problem to produce canonical two-dimensional coordinates and a dense distance matrix.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors propose a geometry-first framework for reconstructing intrinsic single-cell spatial geometry without the listed auxiliary requirements.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments, including cross-section generalization.

The authors report consistent improvements in global distance preservation, local neighborhood fidelity, and spatial distribution alignment compared with strong spatial mapping and deconvolution baselines.

narrative_sequence.summary: Single-cell sequencing offers scale but loses spatial context, whereas spatial transcriptomics retains partial spatial structure at lower resolution.
Existing integration approaches are tied to spot mixtures or fixed spot lattices and coordinate systems, especially limiting unpaired reconstruction.
GEARS learns aligned expression representations and generates local spatial geometries under pose-invariant supervision.
Predictions from overlapping cell subsets are aggregated and converted into global canonical coordinates through distance geometry.
Experiments reportedly show improvements over spatial mapping and deconvolution baselines across several spatial fidelity measures.
